style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: So, before you practice, let's go over all of letter puzzles in a few minutes.
Every rule, every trap. Short, and quick.
First, what do the letters mean?
A bar on top means these are the digits of ONE number. A B is not A times B.
The same letter is always the same digit. Different letters? Only if the question says so.
And the leftmost digit is never zero.
Now, the technique. Four steps, every time.
Write it vertically. Check the units digit. Check the leftmost digit, and the size. And then plug in.
The ones column is special. Nothing carries into it.
But in any other column, there may be a carry. Then Y can be nine. Two X nine, plus Y four... Y is nine.
Two numbers carry zero or one. Three or four numbers can carry more. Seven plus seven plus nine is twenty-three... so you carry two.
Now, the leftmost digit.
You add TWO numbers and get more digits? Then the leading digit is one.
But that's only for two numbers. Three numbers can start with two.
And estimate the size. It throws out choices fast.
The special digits are zero, one, five and six.
Multiply one of them by itself, and the units digit stays. No other digit does that.
Five times an even number ends in zero, and times an odd number it ends in five. Six times an even number keeps its units digit. Six times twelve, seventy-two.
Every letter question can be solved by plugging in.
Two choices survive? Try a third number.
And flip a subtraction into an addition, and a division into a multiplication. It's easier to see.
The algebraic form gives you facts that come back again and again.
A number minus its reversal is divisible by nine. With three digits, it's divisible by ninety-nine... and the middle digit is nine.
Triple digits are divisible by three and by thirty-seven. And B B B B over B B is always one hundred one.
Now, products and powers.
Two-digit times two-digit gives four digits... or three.
The units digits of powers repeat in a cycle. So find where you land in the cycle.
Largest or smallest, with a given digit sum.
For the largest, big digits on the left. For the smallest, one first, then zeros, and the big digits on the right.
So, before you practice, always ask yourself:
The common traps: forgetting the carry, a leading zero, and using the leading-digit-one rule with more than two numbers.
And a matching last digit is not a full proof. Check the size too. Okay... go practice.
